title: Abu Simbel
objective: After this level you can describe the temples of Abu Simbel and how they were moved.
summary: Ramesses II carved two temples into the cliffs at Abu Simbel. In the 1960s, a UNESCO-led campaign cut them into blocks and rebuilt them above the rising lake of the Aswan High Dam.

cards.headline: Twice a year, sunrise reaches the back of a temple cut deep into rock.
cards.body: At Abu Simbel, on about February 22 and October 22, the first rays of the morning sun run the whole length of Ramesses II’s great temple and light its innermost shrine. It still happens. Just not where the temple was built.

cards.headline: Four guards, all named Ramesses
cards.body: Ramesses built two temples at Abu Simbel. The great temple, for the sun gods Amon-Re and Re-Horakhte, has four seated figures of Ramesses at its entrance, each 20 metres tall. The smaller temple honors his queen, Nefertari, and the goddess Hathor, with 10.5-metre statues of king and queen. Visitors met the king four times before they got through the door.

cards.headline: A lake on the way
cards.body: Then came the Aswan High Dam, and its new reservoir was set to drown Abu Simbel. In 1960, UNESCO launched an international campaign to save the monuments of Nubia. Sun and sand the temples could handle. Water was another matter.

cards.headline: Moving a mountain
cards.body: Between 1963 and 1968, engineers and scientists, funded by more than 50 countries, cut away the top of the cliff, sawed both temples into some 16,000 blocks and rebuilt them on high ground more than 60 metres above the old site. A jigsaw puzzle made of temple, reassembled uphill.

cards.headline: Abu Simbel: saved
learned: Ramesses II built two temples at Abu Simbel
Four 20-metre Ramesses guard the great temple
The Aswan High Dam’s lake threatened them
In the 1960s they were cut into blocks and rebuilt higher up

questions.prompt: What sits at the entrance of the great temple at Abu Simbel?

options.label: Two sphinxes with Ramesses’ face
options.rationale: The entrance has seated figures, not sphinxes.

options.label: Four seated figures of Ramesses II
Statues of Nefertari and Hathor
options.rationale: Those belong with the smaller temple.

options.label: A pair of stone obelisks
options.rationale: The facade is carved with colossal seated figures.

questions.explanation: Four 20-metre seated figures of Ramesses flank the great temple’s entrance, two on each side.

questions.prompt: Why were the Abu Simbel temples cut into blocks in the 1960s?

options.label: To ship them to museums abroad
options.rationale: They were rebuilt nearby, in Egypt.

options.label: The Aswan High Dam’s reservoir would have flooded them
An earthquake had cracked the cliff behind the temples
To find tombs hidden underneath
options.rationale: The goal was to save the temples.

questions.explanation: The new lake behind the Aswan High Dam would have drowned them, so they were moved more than 60 metres higher.

questions.prompt: At Abu Simbel, sunrise lights the temple’s innermost shrine; from Level 34, what did Egyptians believe a temple’s shrine held?

options.label: The king’s mummy, sealed for eternity
options.rationale: Kings were buried in tombs, not temple shrines.

options.label: The god, living within its statue
The temple’s gold and taxes
options.rationale: The shrine was the god’s home, not a treasury.

questions.explanation: A temple was its god’s house, and Egyptians believed the god lived within its statue in a shrine deep inside.
